critical_conditions.statement: Like other tools specialized to code search, ripgrep defaults to [recursive search](GUIDE.md#recursive-search) and does [automatic filtering](GUIDE.md#automatic-filtering). Namely, ripgrep won't search files ignored by your `.gitignore`/`.ignore`/`.rgignore` files, it won't search hidden files and it won't search binary files. Automatic filtering can be disabled with `rg -uuu`.

gold_cases.query: Find ignored, hidden and binary files with ripgrep; what default filtering must be disabled?

critical_conditions.statement: ripgrep can [search specific types of files](GUIDE.md#manual-filtering-file-types). For example, `rg -tpy foo` limits your search to Python files and `rg -Tjs foo` excludes JavaScript files from your search. ripgrep can be taught about new file types with custom matching rules.

gold_cases.query: Search Python files while excluding JavaScript using ripgrep file types.

critical_conditions.statement: ripgrep has optional support for switching its regex engine to use PCRE2. Among other things, this makes it possible to use look-around and backreferences in your patterns, which are not supported in ripgrep's default regex engine. PCRE2 support can be enabled with `-P/--pcre2` (use PCRE2 always) or `--auto-hybrid-regex` (use PCRE2 only if needed). An alternative syntax is provided via the `--engine (default|pcre2|auto)` option.

gold_cases.query: Use look-around and backreferences: which regex engine must be enabled?

critical_conditions.statement: ripgrep supports [searching files in text encodings](GUIDE.md#file-encoding) other than UTF-8, such as UTF-16, latin-1, GBK, EUC-JP, Shift_JIS and more. (Some support for automatically detecting UTF-16 is provided. Other text encodings must be specifically specified with the `-E/--encoding` flag.)

gold_cases.query: Search a Shift_JIS file; when does encoding need to be specified?

critical_conditions.statement: ripgrep supports searching files compressed in a common format (brotli, bzip2, gzip, lz4, lzma, xz, or zstandard) with the `-z/--search-zip` flag.

gold_cases.query: Search inside gzip and zstandard compressed files.

critical_conditions.statement: You need a portable and ubiquitous tool. While ripgrep works on Windows, macOS and Linux, it is not ubiquitous and it does not conform to any standard such as POSIX. The best tool for this job is good old grep.

gold_cases.query: Can a POSIX script depend on ripgrep being ubiquitous and standards conforming?

critical_conditions.statement: It supports searching with either memory maps or by searching incrementally with an intermediate buffer. The former is better for single files and the latter is better for large directories. ripgrep chooses the best searching strategy for you automatically.

gold_cases.query: How are memory maps versus incremental buffers chosen for a large directory?

critical_conditions.statement: Enabling the PCRE2 feature works with a stable Rust compiler and will attempt to automatically find and link with your system's PCRE2 library via `pkg-config`. If one doesn't exist, then ripgrep will build PCRE2 from source using your system's C compiler and then statically link it into the final executable. Static linking can be forced even when there is an available PCRE2 system library by either building ripgrep with the MUSL target or by setting `PCRE2_SYS_STATIC=1`.

gold_cases.query: Force static PCRE2 linking even when the system library exists.

cases.query: Find ignored, hidden and binary files with ripgrep; what default filtering must be disabled?
cases.quote:
* Like other tools specialized to code search, ripgrep defaults to
  [recursive search](GUIDE.md#recursive-search) and does [automatic
  filtering](GUIDE.md#automatic-filtering). Namely, ripgrep won't search files
  ignored by your `.gitignore`/`.ignore`/`.rgignore` files, it won't search
  hidden files and it won't search binary files. Automatic filtering can be
  disabled with `rg -uuu`.
cases.statement: Like other tools specialized to code search, ripgrep defaults to [recursive search](GUIDE.md#recursive-search) and does [automatic filtering](GUIDE.md#automatic-filtering). Namely, ripgrep won't search files ignored by your `.gitignore`/`.ignore`/`.rgignore` files, it won't search hidden files and it won't search binary files. Automatic filtering can be disabled with `rg -uuu`.

cases.query: Search Python files while excluding JavaScript using ripgrep file types.

  foo` excludes JavaScript files from your search. ripgrep can be taught about
  new file types with custom matching rules.

cases.subject: types

cases.query: Use look-around and backreferences: which regex engine must be enabled?
cases.quote:
* ripgrep has optional support for switching its regex engine to use PCRE2.
  Among other things, this makes it possible to use look-around and
  backreferences in your patterns, which are not supported in ripgrep's default
  regex engine. PCRE2 support can be enabled with `-P/--pcre2` (use PCRE2
  always) or `--auto-hybrid-regex` (use PCRE2 only if needed). An alternative
  syntax is provided via the `--engine (default|pcre2|auto)` option.

cases.query: Can a POSIX script depend on ripgrep being ubiquitous and standards conforming?
cases.quote:
* You need a portable and ubiquitous tool. While ripgrep works on Windows,
  macOS and Linux, it is not ubiquitous and it does not conform to any
  standard such as POSIX. The best tool for this job is good old grep.

  latter is better for large directories. ripgrep chooses the best searching
  strategy for you automatically.

cases.query: Force static PCRE2 linking even when the system library exists.
cases.quote:
Enabling the PCRE2 feature works with a stable Rust compiler and will
attempt to automatically find and link with your system's PCRE2 library via
`pkg-config`. If one doesn't exist, then ripgrep will build PCRE2 from source
using your system's C compiler and then statically link it into the final
executable. Static linking can be forced even when there is an available PCRE2
system library by either building ripgrep with the MUSL target or by setting
`PCRE2_SYS_STATIC=1`.
cases.statement: Enabling the PCRE2 feature works with a stable Rust compiler and will attempt to automatically find and link with your system's PCRE2 library via `pkg-config`. If one doesn't exist, then ripgrep will build PCRE2 from source using your system's C compiler and then statically link it into the final executable. Static linking can be forced even when there is an available PCRE2 system library by either building ripgrep with the MUSL target or by setting `PCRE2_SYS_STATIC=1`.
cases.subject: pcre2-linking

critical_conditions.statement: By default, *fd* does not search hidden directories and does not show hidden files in the search results. To disable this behavior, we can use the `-H` (or `--hidden`) option:

gold_cases.query: Find hidden files and directories with fd.

critical_conditions.statement: If we work in a directory that is a Git repository (or includes Git repositories), *fd* does not search folders (and does not show files) that match one of the `.gitignore` patterns. To disable this behavior, we can use the `-I` (or `--no-ignore`) option:

gold_cases.query: Search folders ignored by .gitignore while inside a Git repository.

critical_conditions.statement: By default, *fd* only matches the filename of each file. However, using the `--full-path` or `-p` option, you can match against the full path.

gold_cases.query: Match the full file path rather than only the filename.

critical_conditions.statement: The `-x`/`--exec` option runs an external command *for each of the search results* (in parallel). * The `-X`/`--exec-batch` option launches the external command once, with *all search results as arguments*.

gold_cases.query: Run one command for every result or a single command with all results.

critical_conditions.statement: For `-x`/`--exec`, you can control the number of parallel jobs by using the `-j`/`--threads` option. Use `--threads=1` for serial execution.

gold_cases.query: Run external commands serially instead of in parallel.

critical_conditions.statement: If you want `fd` to ignore these patterns globally, you can put them in `fd`'s global ignore file. This is usually located in `~/.config/fd/ignore` in macOS or Linux, and `%APPDATA%\fd\ignore` in Windows.

gold_cases.query: Where are global ignore files located on Windows and Linux?

critical_conditions.statement: Shell `alias`es and shell functions can not be used for command execution via `fd -x` or `fd -X`. In `zsh`, you can make the alias global via `alias -g myalias="…"`. In `bash`, you can use `export -f my_function` to make available to child processes. You would still need to call `fd -x bash -c 'my_function "$1"' bash`. For other use cases or shells, use a (temporary) shell script.

gold_cases.query: Use shell functions with fd -x, preserving the documented shell-specific requirements.

critical_conditions.statement: `--null-input` / `-n`: Don't read any input at all. Instead, the filter is run once using `null` as the input. This is useful when using jq as a simple calculator or to construct JSON data from scratch.

gold_cases.query: Construct JSON from scratch without reading any input.

critical_conditions.statement: `--raw-input` / `-R`: Don't parse the input as JSON. Instead, each line of text is passed to the filter as a string. If combined with `--slurp`, then the entire input is passed to the filter as a single long string.

gold_cases.query: Read raw input lines; what changes when --slurp is combined with --raw-input?

critical_conditions.statement: `--raw-output` / `-r`: With this option, if the filter's result is a string then it will be written directly to standard output rather than being formatted as a JSON string with quotes. This can be useful for making jq filters talk to non-JSON-based systems.

gold_cases.query: When does --raw-output print unquoted text instead of JSON?

critical_conditions.statement: `--raw-output0`: Like `-r` but jq will print NUL instead of newline after each output. This can be useful when the values being output can contain newlines. When the output value contains NUL, jq exits with non-zero code.

gold_cases.query: Use NUL-separated output and account for a value that contains NUL.

critical_conditions.statement: `--join-output` / `-j`: Like `-r` but jq won't print a newline after each output.

gold_cases.query: Produce raw output without a newline after each result.

critical_conditions.statement: `--ascii-output` / `-a`: jq usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode codepoints as UTF-8, even if the input specified them as escape sequences (like "\u03bc"). Using this option, you can force jq to produce pure ASCII output with every non-ASCII character replaced with the equivalent escape sequence.

gold_cases.query: Force non-ASCII Unicode characters into ASCII escape sequences.

critical_conditions.statement: `--color-output` / `-C` and `--monochrome-output` / `-M`: By default, jq outputs colored JSON if writing to a terminal. You can force it to produce color even if writing to a pipe or a file using `-C`, and disable color with `-M`. When the `NO_COLOR` environment variable is not empty, jq disables colored output by default, but you can enable it by `-C`.

gold_cases.query: Force colored JSON with NO_COLOR set and explain default terminal behavior.

critical_conditions.statement: `--exit-status` / `-e`: Sets the exit status of jq to 0 if the last output value was neither `false` nor `null`, 1 if the last output value was either `false` or `null`, or 4 if no valid result was ever produced. Normally jq exits with 2 if there was any usage problem or system error, 3 if there was a jq program compile error, or 0 if the jq program ran.

gold_cases.query: Use --exit-status: distinguish false, null, no output, usage error and compile error.

cases.query: Construct JSON from scratch without reading any input.
cases.quote:
* `--null-input` / `-n`:

        Don't read any input at all. Instead, the filter is run once
        using `null` as the input. This is useful when using jq as a
        simple calculator or to construct JSON data from scratch.
cases.statement: `--null-input` / `-n`: Don't read any input at all. Instead, the filter is run once using `null` as the input. This is useful when using jq as a simple calculator or to construct JSON data from scratch.

cases.query: Read raw input lines; what changes when --slurp is combined with --raw-input?
cases.quote:
* `--raw-input` / `-R`:

        Don't parse the input as JSON. Instead, each line of text is
        passed to the filter as a string. If combined with `--slurp`,
        then the entire input is passed to the filter as a single long
        string.
cases.statement: `--raw-input` / `-R`: Don't parse the input as JSON. Instead, each line of text is passed to the filter as a string. If combined with `--slurp`, then the entire input is passed to the filter as a single long string.
cases.subject: raw-slurp

cases.query: When does --raw-output print unquoted text instead of JSON?
cases.quote:
* `--raw-output` / `-r`:

        With this option, if the filter's result is a string then it
        will be written directly to standard output rather than being
        formatted as a JSON string with quotes. This can be useful for
        making jq filters talk to non-JSON-based systems.
cases.statement: `--raw-output` / `-r`: With this option, if the filter's result is a string then it will be written directly to standard output rather than being formatted as a JSON string with quotes. This can be useful for making jq filters talk to non-JSON-based systems.
cases.subject: raw-output

cases.quote:

cases.statement: `--raw-output0`: Like `-r` but jq will print NUL instead of newline after each output. This can be useful when the values being output can contain newlines. When the output value contains NUL, jq exits with non-zero code.

cases.query: Force non-ASCII Unicode characters into ASCII escape sequences.
cases.quote:
* `--ascii-output` / `-a`:

        jq usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode codepoints as UTF-8, even
        if the input specified them as escape sequences (like
        "\u03bc"). Using this option, you can force jq to produce pure
        ASCII output with every non-ASCII character replaced with the
        equivalent escape sequence.
cases.statement: `--ascii-output` / `-a`: jq usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode codepoints as UTF-8, even if the input specified them as escape sequences (like "\u03bc"). Using this option, you can force jq to produce pure ASCII output with every non-ASCII character replaced with the equivalent escape sequence.
cases.subject: ascii-output

cases.query: Force colored JSON with NO_COLOR set and explain default terminal behavior.
cases.quote:
* `--color-output` / `-C` and `--monochrome-output` / `-M`:

        By default, jq outputs colored JSON if writing to a
        terminal. You can force it to produce color even if writing to
        a pipe or a file using `-C`, and disable color with `-M`.
        When the `NO_COLOR` environment variable is not empty, jq disables
        colored output by default, but you can enable it by `-C`.

cases.subject: color

cases.query: Use --exit-status: distinguish false, null, no output, usage error and compile error.
cases.quote:
* `--exit-status` / `-e`:

        Sets the exit status of jq to 0 if the last output value was
        neither `false` nor `null`, 1 if the last output value was
        either `false` or `null`, or 4 if no valid result was ever
        produced.  Normally jq exits with 2 if there was any usage
        problem or system error, 3 if there was a jq program compile
        error, or 0 if the jq program ran.
